title: Exploring Musicians’ Perspectives on Decent Work, Creativity, and Well-Being
abstract: This study, grounded in the psychology of working theory (PWT) and self-determination theory (SDT), examined how working conditions shape musicians’ experiences of decent work, intrinsic motivation, artistic identity, creative engagement, and psychological well-being. Sixteen in-depth interviews were conducted with Portuguese musicians, including both freelancers and those with stable contracts. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four overarching themes: (a) job security and precarity, (b) intrinsic motivation, autonomy, and creative engagement, (c) artistic identity and purpose, and (d) well-being and mental health. The findings show that freelance instability undermines security, constrains creative risk-taking, and increases stress, whereas financial and institutional stability supports intrinsic motivation, reinforces artistic identity, and enables creative exploration. Features associated with intrinsic motivation, voluntary engagement, persistence, and psychological investment in creative tasks were observed across both groups. Autonomy itself sustained engagement for some freelancers, highlighting personal resilience and self-directed creativity. The results underscore the interplay between structural conditions (PWT) and individual motivations (SDT), showing that sustainable work environments foster well-being and high-quality creative output. The study provides practical implications for policies, education, and organizational strategies to support healthier, more productive artistic ecosystems.

title: Perceived Usability of Music-Genre Labels in Musical-Taste Research
abstract:
Quantitative research on musical tastes has largely relied on genre-based analyses. However, evidence regarding the usability of such labels is lacking. In the present study, we assessed the extent to which individuals feel able to describe their musical tastes using music-genre labels. Our study was conducted as part of the
                     Étude Longitudinale par Internet Pour les Sciences Sociales 
                    , a nationwide research project conducted in France. A total of 1,721 participants (51.5% female) were asked to evaluate the usability of music-genre labels. Results showed that a majority of respondents were uncomfortable with the use of music-genre labels, irrespective of their education, income, and sex. Age was associated with the assessment of music-genre labels, with older people reporting the greatest difficulty using such labels. Overall, our findings suggest that reliance on music-genre labels in research on musical preferences may raise usability and validity concerns.

title: High School Music Participation: The Role of Identity, Value, Expectancy, and Cost
abstract: While secondary music programs enjoy participation from many students, school music enrollment often does not reflect the demographics of the broader student population. This study examined how high-school students’ musical identities and sociocognitive beliefs influenced their intentions to enroll in high-school music classes. Drawing on situated expectancy-value theory, we developed a model of how musical identity and expectancy-value constructs influence students’ enrollment decisions in three music classes: large ensembles, music technology/production, and piano/guitar. We surveyed 486 students at a large U.S. public high school, measuring musical identity, expectancy-value constructs, and intentions to enroll in each of the three class contexts. Structural equation models showed musical identity positively predicted expectancy and value; expectancy negatively predicted cost; and both value and cost predicted enrollment intentions (positively and negatively, respectively). Notably, expectancy influenced intentions only indirectly via cost. Although both value and cost predicted intentions across all class types, cost was more strongly associated with intentions for large ensembles, whereas value was more strongly associated with intentions for music technology/production and piano/guitar. These findings suggest motivational beliefs are context-dependent and deeply interrelated. Music teachers may benefit from considering the context-specific roles of cost, value, and expectancy when recruiting students for classes.
